paras: The lynching of Charles Pierce took place on the night of October 1, 1881, in Bloomington, Illinois, when a crowd reported at 4,000 to 5,000 broke into the McLean County jail and hanged Pierce from a tree near the jail. Pierce, a young prisoner held for horse theft, was accused of shooting jailer Ted Franks to death a few hours earlier. Papers across the country noted that leading citizens had joined the mob, and editors later cited the case in debates over lynching in the North and the South.

Pierce, about 20, was awaiting trial for stealing a horse and buggy in Bloomington and was said to have confessed after his arrest at Jacksonville. A Jacksonville dispatch said he had used the names Charlie Christ and Henry Pierce, that his real name was Charles Hewlett, and that his early home was Mount Pleasant, Iowa; the Rock Island Argus called him Howlett.

Feeling in Bloomington was also running against the courts, because word had arrived the day before that the Illinois Supreme Court had reversed the death sentence of Patsy Devine for the murder of Aaron Goodfellow.

At about 6 or 6:30 p.m., as Franks moved Pierce from one cell to another, Pierce was said to have snatched the jailer's pistol and shot him three times, the last shot through the heart. According to the Rock Island Argus, other prisoners then seized and held him. By 8 o'clock a crowd of men, women and boys surrounded the jail demanding him.

For about two hours the sheriff and police fought at the jail door, and State's Attorney R. B. Porter and his predecessor Fifer were hooted down with cries that 'justice and the courts are a farce.' Lieutenant Governor John M. Hamilton telegraphed Governor S. M. Cullom that the sheriff was powerless; the militia company could not be assembled.

With axes and sledge-hammers the crowd broke through the jail doors, put a rope around Pierce's neck and dragged him through the mud to a tree near the jail. Accounts named the tree variously as a maple, an elm, or a locust at the corner of Market and Centre Streets. Officer Bailey cut the rope the first time Pierce was raised, but the crowd hoisted him again, and women in the crowd waved handkerchiefs and cheered. After about thirty minutes the body was cut down and taken by the coroner, and the crowd, which had also called for Devine, dispersed without touching him.

On October 3 a coroner's jury found that Pierce died by hanging at the hands of a mob whose members were unknown to the jury, between 8 and 10 p.m. on October 1. No report of arrests or prosecution of anyone in the mob appears in the coverage. On Sunday thousands viewed the jail and the body, and a card tacked to the tree urged the good people to stand by 'the boys that did it.'

Wire reports appeared on October 2 in St. Paul and Memphis under heads such as 'Murder and Mob Law,' calling Pierce 'the murderer,' and briefs ran in weeklies as far as Alabama and South Carolina through mid-October. The Chicago Tribune printed the fullest coverage, reporting that while all deprecated the method there seemed no regret at Pierce's death. A Chicago dispatch reprinted in Maine stressed that 'some of the best citizens' led the mob, and a Kansas version said there was 'no element of ruffianism' in the crowd.

Democratic and Southern editors turned the case against Republican critics of the South: a Pittsburgh Post editorial reprinted in Ohio told the Tribune to look 'nearer home,' and a Tennessee paper wrote that lynch law did not prevail in the South alone. The Tribune in turn cited the Bloomington mob's motto, 'The law is a farce,' as evidence that criminal justice was failing, an editorial reprinted in Canton, Illinois. None of the reports described Pierce's race or the race of anyone involved.

Accounts differ on the crowd's size, from 4,000 or 5,000 in the wire reports to 'some 2,000' in a later digest, and one weekly dated the shooting September 30, though the coroner's verdict places the hanging on October 1.

bases: A crowd broke into the McLean County jail, took Charles Pierce from the officers and hanged him from a tree near the jail (A1, A5, A9).

Pierce was hanged by a crowd numbered in the thousands that broke open the jail against the sheriff and police, in retaliation for his shooting of the jailer and with cries that 'the courts are a farce' (A1, A4, A5, A9); no article gives his race.
Independent dispatches in the Chicago Tribune, the Rock Island Argus and the wire agree on the shooting, the jail break and the hanging, and the coroner's jury verdict confirms it (A1, A5, A8, A9).

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune called the shooting a 'horrible tragedy', called Pierce 'the murderer' and 'the assassin', and reported that while all deprecated the method there was no regret at his death.
Wire versions ran under heads such as 'Murder and Mob Law' and 'Western Style of Serving Murderers', stressing the 'best citizens' among the lynchers.
The Emporia Weekly News version said there was 'no element of ruffianism' and the crowd was sober but determined.

Democratic and Southern papers used Bloomington to answer Republican criticism of 'the lawless and murderous South'; the Tribune later blamed failures of criminal justice for the mob's motto 'The law is a farce'.
